questions.passage: Should hospitals adopt a policy of only hiring staff who have completed a specific cultural competency training programme?
questions.question: Which is the strongest argument FOR this policy?
options: Culturally competent care improves health outcomes and reduces disparities for diverse patient populations
Some patients feel misunderstood by healthcare providers from different cultural backgrounds
The training programme is well-designed and well-reviewed
Other hospitals have already adopted similar policies
questions.correct: Culturally competent care improves health outcomes and reduces disparities for diverse patient populations
questions.explanation: This provides evidence-based justification linking cultural competency directly to measurable patient outcomes. The other options are weaker — patient feelings are less concrete, programme quality doesn't mandate hiring, and others' actions don't establish this as best practice.

questions.passage: In a study of 140 patients: 80 have chronic pain, 55 have depression, 25 have both chronic pain and depression, and 10 have neither condition.
questions.question: How many patients have chronic pain but not depression?
questions.explanation: Chronic pain only = Total chronic pain - Both = 80 - 25 = 55.

questions.passage: Three patients — Jay, Kim, and Leo — are scheduled for MRI scans at 10:00, 11:00, and 12:00. Kim's scan is at a later time than Jay's. Jay's scan is not at 12:00. Leo's scan is at 10:00.
questions.question: What time is Kim's scan?
options: Cannot be determined
questions.explanation: Leo is at 10:00. The remaining times are 11:00 and 12:00. Jay is before Kim, and Jay is not at 12:00, so Jay must be at 11:00 and Kim at 12:00.

questions.passage: All patients on warfarin need regular INR monitoring. Some patients who need INR monitoring also need dose adjustments. All patients whose warfarin dose is adjusted need follow-up appointments.
questions.question: Which conclusion definitely follows?
options: All warfarin patients need follow-up appointments
Some warfarin patients may need follow-up appointments
No warfarin patients need dose adjustments
All patients with follow-up appointments are on warfarin
questions.correct: Some warfarin patients may need follow-up appointments
questions.explanation: Warfarin → INR monitoring. Some needing INR monitoring need dose adjustments. Dose adjustment → follow-up appointment. So some warfarin patients may need follow-up appointments.

questions.passage:
A hospital pharmacy reports:
- Medication error rate fell from 3.2% to 1.1% over 18 months
- A barcode scanning system was introduced at month 6
- Double-checking protocols were implemented at month 12
- Staff training hours increased by 30%
questions.question: Which inference is best supported?
options: Medication errors have been completely eliminated
The barcode scanning system alone reduced errors from 3.2% to 1.1%
The phased introduction of multiple safeguards likely contributed to the progressive reduction in errors
Staff training is unnecessary if barcode scanning is in place
questions.correct: The phased introduction of multiple safeguards likely contributed to the progressive reduction in errors
questions.explanation: Three interventions were introduced at different points over 18 months while errors progressively fell (3.2%→1.1%). It is most reasonable to attribute the sustained improvement to the combination of systems.

questions.passage: A diagnostic test for urinary tract infection (UTI) has a sensitivity of 94% and specificity of 85%. In a GP practice, 15% of women presenting with symptoms actually have a UTI.
questions.question: If a woman tests positive, what is the approximate probability she truly has a UTI?
options: About 30%
About 49%
About 55%
About 70%
questions.explanation: Of 1,000 women: 150 have UTI (141 true positives). 850 don't (127.5 false positives). P(UTI|positive) = 141/(141+127.5) ≈ 52.5%. Closest is 55%.

questions.passage: Of 110 patients at a respiratory clinic: 70 use inhalers, 45 use nebulisers, 15 use both, and 10 use neither device.
questions.question: How many patients use inhalers but not nebulisers?

questions.passage:
A mental health unit tracks restraint use:

| Quarter | Physical Restraint | Seclusion | PRN Medication |
|---------|-------------------|-----------|----------------|
| Q1 | 25 | 18 | 30 |
| Q2 | 20 | 15 | 28 |
| Q3 | 15 | 12 | 22 |
| Q4 | 10 | 8 | 18 |
questions.question: Which quarter showed the largest single-quarter drop in total restrictive interventions?
options: Q1 to Q2
Q2 to Q3
Q3 to Q4
All quarters showed equal drops
questions.explanation: Q1 total: 25+18+30=73. Q2 total: 20+15+28=63 (drop of 10). Q3 total: 15+12+22=49 (drop of 14). Q4 total: 10+8+18=36 (drop of 13). Q2→Q3 had the largest drop of 14.

questions.passage: Should medical schools use standardised patients (actors) rather than real patients for clinical examinations?
questions.question: Which is the strongest argument AGAINST using standardised patients?
options: Standardised patients cannot replicate the unpredictability and complexity of real clinical presentations
Real patients may feel uncomfortable being examined by students
Standardised patient programmes are expensive to maintain
Students may find it harder to build rapport with actors
questions.correct: Standardised patients cannot replicate the unpredictability and complexity of real clinical presentations
questions.explanation: Real patients present with unpredictable symptoms, emotional states, and comorbidities that actors cannot fully simulate. This is the most significant educational drawback. The other options are less compelling.
